title: Paramitas
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the six paramitas on the seventh day of sesshin, reading one verse for each from Thokme Zongpo's 37 Practices of a Bodhisattva, in Ken MacLeod's translation Reflections on Silver River, alongside stanzas from the Prajnaparamita Eight Thousand Line Sutra. Norman opens with Ken's account of a miserable retreat, where a prayer to accept illness, recovery, or death led him to lean against a tree beneath blooming acacias and find peace in the pain. Generosity draws on the Jataka tales of the Buddha giving his body to a tigress and leaping into a fire as a rabbit, and on the fiction of owning land. Patience turns on the idea that a person who hurts you is a treasure. Norman closes with Emily Dickinson's lines about easing one life the aching.

sentences.text: We're going pretty fast, right?
We're sitting here on the last full day of our seven-day sesshin.
What happened?
Where are we now?
Where are we going?
Well, I think we all know that this is a bodhisattva path, a full life of commitment and of joy.
Bodhisattvas practice upaya, skillful means.
Skillful means is flexibility, openness, imagination, the capacity to improvise and turn things around in all situations.
Practicing upaya, bodhisattvas use whatever comes to hand, whatever they are given, whatever appears in front of them to further their path toward awakening through benefiting beings.
If a person needs medicine, a bodhisattva appears as a doctor or nurse.
If a person needs emotional healing, a bodhisattva will appear as a psychotherapist.
If people need food, bodhisattvas appear as farmers and truck drivers and grocery store clerks.

If there's a need for legal services, laundry services, plumbing, bike repair, childcare, entertainment, poetry or music, cleaning out flues or gathering news or garbage disposal, protecting plants and animals, cleaning up ecologically wasted areas, giving birth to and taking care of children, counting birds or fish for surveys, studying air or land or sea, burying people or digging them up for archaeological purposes, making clothes, repairing shoes or computers or cars or refrigerators, doing hair, doing nails, communicating, cleaning houses, painting signs, making signs, serving in the government or making sure that good government officials are elected, bodhisattvas are there to help.
But bodhisattvas know that whatever social role they happen to be occupying, given to them by their karma, this is not actually who they are and it is not actually what they're doing.
They are bodhisattvas going on and on and on in their effort to practice for the benefit of others.
This is their love and their passion and this is their joy.
Bodhisattvas are characterized by vows.
They take many vows, infinite vows to benefit infinite beings and to engage infinite practices.
Whatever practice appears to them they take it up, because they have an infinite need to understand and an infinite need to deepen and extend their range.
But bodhisattva practice is mostly broadly defined by the six paramitas of generosity, ethical conduct, patience, joyful effort, meditation and wisdom.
The word paramita, which is usually translated as perfection, means to go beyond, to leap beyond.
So in our chant we say wisdom beyond wisdom, prajna paramita.
Wisdom is one thing, it's a good thing.
But wisdom beyond wisdom, that's another thing.
Generosity is really good, but generosity beyond generosity, that's something else.
Like with any craft or profession that you might practice thoughtfully for an entire lifetime, you go beyond that profession.
You arrive at some place of understanding life through the ongoing study of that profession.
It's the same with the six paramitas.
Generosity goes beyond mere giving to a full appreciation of the bounty inherent in life.
Ethical conduct goes beyond mere moral constraint to boundless love.
Joyful effort goes beyond effort to all-inclusive, ceaseless, beneficial activity.
Patience goes beyond gentle forbearance to the deep appreciation of sorrow and pain.
And meditation goes beyond meditation to the total presence with the truth of things.
And wisdom goes beyond probity and perceptiveness to the profound recognition of emptiness, which means a complete interconnection in love.
Self and other are useful illusions.
Self and other are empty.
Everything flows freely, in and out, in and out.
Of the six paramitas, prajnaparamita is the most important, and its sweet fragrance perfumes all the others.
Giving, ethical conduct, patience, joyful effort, meditation are all empty of any accomplishment, empty of any distinguishing characteristics.
So it means every moment is a moment bursting full of generosity, ethical conduct, patience and so on.
What this means for us, practically speaking, is that we are practicing giving and so on without any idea that we're doing such a thing.
We give without thinking we're giving, without thinking that there's a recipient or a gift.
And we are ethical without thinking that we're ethical and without condemning someone else because we think they aren't.
There is a purity and an innocence to the practice of bodhisattvas.
They just keep on doing what they do with great passion and insistence, no matter what.
And they don't even know what they're doing.
And they certainly make no claims to be doing anything at all.
To practice in that spirit, in that way, is their deep commitment and their joy.
We've been talking about the six paramitas for many decades, many centuries, a couple of millennia.
And we will go on talking about them until the end of time, if time ever ends.
Today I want to talk about them again, this time by sharing a few verses with you.

I'll share some short verses from a book called *Reflections on Silver River*, which is a translation of a Tibetan text by a friend of mine, Ken MacLeod, a text of Thokme Zongpo, a 13th century Tibetan master.
The text is also called *37 Practices of a Bodhisattva*: one practice, one verse, 37 verses.
And six of those verses are about the six paramitas.
And also I'll quote a few stanzas from verses about the paramitas found in the Prajnaparamita Eight Thousand Line Sutra, which is the sutra I quoted on the first day of sesshin.
I want to read you first a little bit from Ken's introduction, describing a time when he first encountered the teachings of Thokme Zongpo Rinpoche.
Ken was on a long retreat, and he was having a really hard time.

I've been observing people practicing Tibetan Buddhism over many, many decades, and it seems to me that Dharma practice can be very dramatic sometimes, especially if you're practicing Tibetan Buddhism.
Years ago, in the time that Ken is writing about, it was an introduction.
And maybe it's still true, I don't know.
But in those days, it was not at all unusual for practitioners of Tibetan Buddhism to have some very dramatic and colorful things happen to them.
Sometimes these things were really terrible, like they would have strange, unexplained illnesses, or sudden, unbelievable reversals of fortune.
They would lose millions of dollars, or somebody would give them millions of dollars.
Things like that happen.
And actually this happened, sadly, to one of my closest friends, who was one of the early practitioners of Tibetan Buddhism.
In the early days, when the great gurus that are now memories were still living, my friend's name was Marty Watten, and we were very close friends.
I knew everybody in his family, his parents, his cousin Barrett Watten, who's one of my oldest colleagues in poetry.
Marty and I actually had a little gardening business together, and we would be working in the gardens, yakking and yakking all day long, dharma, dharma, dharma.
And Marty was an unbelievable talker.
When I say yakking, yakking, mostly he was yakking, yakking.
I was getting in a few words when I could.
He was amazing.
And he went on a long retreat in France.
And he was sitting, as they do, in this little meditation hut, minding his own business, meditating.
And one day he keeled over, face onto a pillow, and died.
Completely shocking.
And he was in his forties.
And nobody knew he was sick.
Nobody had any idea quite what had happened.
And we found out about this in one of our early sesshins.
The first?
Yeah, we were by Vancouver, and I'm sure some of you might have been in that sesshin.
I don't know how, in those days, before cell phones and email, how did I find out about it?
But somehow in this sesshin, I got word.
I was totally blown away by the fact that my dear friend was suddenly dead in the middle of a retreat.
It was pretty shocking.
Not to worry.
Our practice is not like that.
Anyway, Ken was having a kind of similar experience, although he did not die, the first time he encountered Thokme Zangpo's teaching.
And it's an interesting thing that he writes here.
I want to read it for you.
So he's in a retreat.
*The intensity of practice in the retreat brought up deep-seated blocks that broke me physically and emotionally.
Often I was too ill to do the assigned practices.
And nothing I read helped, nor did any of the advice I received from my teacher or our retreat director.
All I could do was endure the physical pain and emotional misery as best I could.
I tried, without much success, to keep my mind from running amok.
And not knowing what else to do, I turned to taking and sending practice,* which we know about.
*A practice I knew well.
In Kongtrul's commentary, a text I had translated before the retreat, I came across a strange prayer, which happens to have been written by Thokme Zongpo.
And here's the prayer.*
*If it is better for me to be ill, give me the energy to be ill.
If it is better for me to recover, give me the energy to recover.
If it is better for me to die, give me the energy to die.*
*Well, this prayer really spoke to me now.
Physically I was beyond miserable, and emotionally I was in even worse shape.
I was afraid too, because I did not see how I could go on.
I kept hoping for a way out, something, anything, that would dispel the pain and the depression.
The prayer did not alleviate any of my physical or emotional distress, but I said it over and over again, struggling to accept what was happening to me.
I continued the practice of taking and sending, because it is a practice you can do even when you are extremely ill or upset, or both.
And then something happened.*
*To this day I am not sure what changed, but I do know that I just gave up on my life.
I gave up any hope that I would ever be happy or well again, or that I would ever be enlightened or awakened, or whatever you want to call it.
These possibilities were so remote as to be utterly non-existent.
One spring day I stumbled out of my room for some fresh air.
I could barely stand and had to lean against a tree for support.
The acacia trees were in flower, white blossoms against a clear blue sky.
The warmth of the sun dispelled the constant chill of our cinder block cells.
As I looked around I felt quiet in the joy of the moment.
And at peace in the pain.
Then it hit me.
This was the point of practice.
Nothing more.
Life presents you with different experiences.
Every experience has infinite dimensions.
Can you experience all of them without struggling against any of them?
If you can, then suffering comes to an end.*
*So obvious, so simple, so deep, and so wonderful.*
So that's how Ken got interested in Thokme Zongpo Rinpoche, and then he went on to translate this text.
This is verse 25, the first verse about the paramitas.
*If those who want to be awake have to give even their bodies, what need is there to talk about things that you simply own?
Be generous without looking for any return or result.
This is the practice of a Bodhisattva.*
And every one of the verses ends with that phrase, this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
This one is about Dhanaparamita, generosity.
This thing about giving up bodies has to do with traditional Buddhist stories about bodhisattvas whose passion to benefit beings caused them to literally give up their bodies.
There's a Jataka story about the Buddha in a past life offering his body as food for a starving tigress and her cubs.
In another story, the Buddha in a past life is born as a rabbit who joyfully leaps into a campfire because the hunter couldn't find any game and was hungry.
And there are many, many stories like this.
In fact, this is one of the main themes of the Jataka stories.
Such stories are meant to express the extremity and thoroughness of the bodhisattva's love and concern for others.
Others are more important to the bodhisattva than oneself.
The stories, I think, are also meant to show how attached we are and identified we are with our body, how much fear we have about and within our body.
And bodhisattvas become free of this fear.

The bodhisattva practices deeply within and about the body and in doing so truly appreciates and understands the body, its radical vulnerability and its empty nature, dropping the body and mind, as Dogen says.
This enables the bodhisattva to be generous without holding anything back.
The style of Thokme Zongpo's words in this text is not ornate or particularly lofty.
It's plain and simple and to the point.

He's saying in so many words, well, if bodhisattvas are giving up their own bodies for others, how can you be worried about some little property you think you own and you're worried about giving that up?
There is no ownership.
It's just a misunderstanding.
You can imagine, in the old days when the white people came to Washington State and tried to explain to the native peoples about private property and the ownership of land, you can imagine.
I'm trying to explain that concept.
And the people were looking at one another and saying, you know, these pale faces are more fantastical than we thought.
Owning land, what a concept.
A friend of mine has a beautiful big house overlooking the Pacific and he says, gee, I feel so guilty.
And I would say, don't worry, it's very temporary.
Once you take as fiction, once you take as real, the fiction of ownership, actual generosity becomes really, really difficult.
To practice Dhanaparamita, the perfection of generosity, you have to stop owning anything, even your body.
If it appears conventionally that you own something, as it does, you have to keep reminding yourself, no, that's not actually the case.
Then you can be generous without looking for any return, because there really is no generosity.
You're only sharing what never really belonged to you in the first place.
*Be generous without looking for any return or result,* Thokme Zangpo writes.
It might not be that hard to give up return, but it might be harder to give up result.
Maybe I don't need to get credit for my generosity, maybe that's not such a big deal.
But at least if I'm going to be generous, it better help.
Right?
Better produce some good.
There should be some result here.
The perfection of generosity requires that we forget about results.
We just give, that's all.
And we should be shocked and surprised if any good comes of it.
So here's the verse that I'll quote from the Prajnaparamita in 8,000 Lines.
*But one who endowed with morality, pure being, becomes unconcerned about anything that may be dear or not dear, if when she renounces head, hands, and feet, her thought remains undejected.
She becomes one who gives up all she has, always uncovered.*
So in this verse, as in so many others, including the ones I quoted some days ago, fear is often an issue.
Because fear goes along with our essential self-clinging, which is the central point of suffering.
And self-clinging depends on our belief in the non-empty nature of self.
Because we cling to self and cling to our ideas, we're afraid.
So to practice Dhanaparamita is to overcome that fear.
Verse 26.
*If you cannot look after yourself because you have no ethical discipline, then your intention to take care of others is just a joke.
Observe ethical behavior without concern for a conventional life.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.*
As we all understand, ethical conduct is really important on a lot of levels.
It's an expression of our desire to love and not harm others.
And we include ourselves in those others.
Ethical conduct, as Thokme Zongpo says, is the main way we take care of ourselves.
We usually think of ethical conduct as a set of restraints.
Don't do this, don't do that.
Thou shalt not this, thou shalt not that.
It just ruins our fun.
We don't like that.
People telling us what to do and constantly organizing us.
We should be able to talk the way we want to talk.
Just say what we feel.
Forget about being polite.
Or even if what we say is true, it doesn't even matter that much.
We just say what we feel like saying now because we like it.
We pride ourselves: I'm just honest.
I just speak my mind.
I'm just blunt.
Yes, ethical conduct does often involve some restraint.
At least in the beginning it does.
But the purpose of that restraint is to take care of our mind.
Cowboys have ragged minds.
Swaggering around makes your mind a little rough.
Which means it's harder to meditate.
It's harder to be present and remember to do your practice.
And if we are bodhisattvas and we're trying to help others out, if that's our chief passion and purpose, then of course we need to take care of ourselves so we can take care of others.
Ethical conduct means we do not intentionally harm others or ourselves by any act of body, speech or mind.
It means we don't let ourselves indulge terrible thoughts even about other people.
We don't run down other people with our speech.
We don't go around stealing their stuff or treating them unfairly.
And we're always trying to ensure, to the best of our ability, that our community, that our government, don't do that kind of stuff either.
Because ethical conduct is personal, but it's also social.
As Tokme's own post-verse points out, sometimes we practice ethical conduct just for conventional reasons: to be a nice, upstanding citizen.
But bodhisattvas don't really care about that.
Their concern is to take care of self and other, no matter how it looks.
So they're not subject to the usual kind of small-minded self-righteousness and conformity that can go with ethical conduct.
The Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines says,
*By morality, those who hanker after calm are lifted up, established in the sphere of those with the ten powers unbroken in their morality.
However many actions of restraint they comply with, they dedicate them to enlightenment for the benefit of all beings.*
So this verse adds two more points to what we've already said.
First, the association of ethical conduct specifically with calmness of mind.
This is really true, which you can observe in your own mind and in the conduct of others.
When you behave unethically, it makes you jumpy and nervous.
Criminals have very jumpy and nervous minds.
They're very vigilant, because they know.
And the same happens to us when we are sloppy in our conduct.
This is bad for your health.
It's bad for your practice.

And the second point that's made here in the verse is the practice of dedication of merit, which we do in every service: dedicating the merit of the chanting we've just done to those in need, to people all over the world, to all sentient beings, to our teachers and ancestors.
Here the idea is that you would practice ethical conduct and dedicate the merit of that practice for the ultimate benefit of others.
Verse 47.
*For bodhisattvas who want to be rich in virtue, a person who hurts you is a precious treasure.
Cultivate patience for everyone without irritation or resentment.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva.*
When we think of patience, we think of being patient with things like jars that won't open, closet doors that won't close.
At least that's how I think of it.
That's my biggest problem with things like that.

It is difficult to be patient with the intractable physical world in which everything is always in some state of falling apart, or at least not working in the way one expected, plus [unclear: "urinary"].
So yes, being patient with and studying the mind in these conditions is certainly a big part of the practice of patience.
But in the classical discussions of kshanti paramita as here, the emphasis is usually on being patient with people, especially when they behave badly, as they so often do.
So this makes perfect sense.
Bodhisattva practice always has to do with loving and caring for others.
So naturally the practice of patience would have to do with being patient with people.
A person who hurts you is a precious treasure.
Who thinks like that?
Bodhisattvas think like that.
They realize that nobody does harmful action on purpose.
Even when they do it on purpose, it's not on purpose, because everyone is driven by their conditioning, just the same way that you and I are.
Everyone is doing what they have come to feel is the thing to do.
And if their actions raise up in us fear, anger, hatred, defensiveness, moral outrage, or a thirst for revenge, this is a good thing.
Because now we have a chance to clarify and purify all of that that was there anyway, but only brought up when this person brought it up for us.
It's hard to get in touch with hatred and the desire for revenge.
You need a special person to evoke that.
They're a treasure to you.
Nasty people are precious.
Nice people are a dime a dozen.
No big deal, nice person.
But a really nasty person is a treasure, a special treasure.
And so we view that nasty person as our teacher.
And if we have righteous indignation, as we sometimes do, it's not against that person.
It's against the greed or the stupidity or the fear or the carelessness that drives that person's behavior.
Sometimes it takes a while to reflect on all this and remind ourselves of what we're doing.
But for bodhisattvas of long, deep training, this is their immediate reaction.
There really is no irritation or resentment.
Just the skillful means for addressing the situation, if indeed it requires address.
Much, much more often than we recognize, the best thing to do is nothing.
Vajramita says,
*When he hears of someone else speaking to him harshly and offensively, the wise bodhisattva remains quite at ease and contented.
He thinks, who speaks?
Who hears?
How?
To whom?
By whom?
The discerning is then devoted to the foremost perfection and patience.*
So isn't that great?
It emphasizes the koan of self and other.
Who actually did say that disturbing thing?
Who actually did hear it?
Isn't the way we think about it and experience such things always, always built on a foundation of the fiction, of the essential solidity of self and others?
But we all understand, perfectly well, that self and others are empty.
Whoops, we just forgot.
We're running away with this.
Maybe we can remember.
Who hurt whom?
And how could there ever be any such thing as hurting?
*Listeners and solitary Buddhas working only for their own welfare, practice as if their heads were on fire.
To help beings, pour your energy into practice.
It is the source of all abilities.
This is the practice of a Bodhisattva.*
So this is a verse on the very virya paramita, the perfection of joyful effort.
Bodhisattvas love to practice.
It's the most fun for them.
It's more fun than going dancing and all this stuff, you know.
They love to practice.
That's why they're a little weird, right?
That's what they love.
They love sesshins and all things of practice, all the aspects of practice.
This is what gives them the most joy.
So they're not doing it as a chore.
They're doing it because they like it.
Well, maybe sometimes it feels like a chore: I have to go, I'm supposed to go.
But mostly it's a joy.
And the joy of practice has everything to do with others, because practice is always with others, always for others.
And the more we practice, the more our capacity for love and heartfelt connections with others increases, which gives us even more joy.
So we love to practice for that reason as well.
In the discourse about the Bodhisattva path, there is the identification of other paths of practice that emphasize individual liberation rather than the benefit of others.
One such practitioner is called a shravaka, a hearer or listener.
Those are people who focus on the early teachings in a fairly linear way and try to put them very literally into practice.
And then there are pratyekabuddhas who practice alone and for their own well-being and not in interchange with others.

So Tokme Zangpo Rinpoche is saying here, if even these kinds of practitioners, whose goals and scope are fairly limited, practice intensely as if their heads were on fire, how much more effort should we bodhisattvas, whose goals for self and other are infinite, how much more intensely should we exert ourselves?
In Prajnaparamita in 8,000 lines: *The Bodhisattva who intends to wander about in birth and death for a long time.* Now let me switch that.
It's a different verse I want to quote, because there are a lot of verses here in this sutra and I'm not reading them all.
I'm just taking the first one on each of them.
So the first one here is,
*They have pure and courageous minds and are linked to other beings and persons when they are practicing the excellent perfection of vigor.
Joyful effort.
As a servant is submissive to a master, so should the firmly wise submit to subjection by all beings.*
I think that's the wrong one.
There's another one, a little mixed up.
I'm toggling back and forth into my...
Yeah, it was the one I had in the beginning.
I was right in the first place.

*The Bodhisattva who intends to wander about in birth and death for a long time, a yogin devoted to the perfection of the Buddha field for the welfare of beings and who does not produce the least thought of fatigue is endowed with the perfection of vigor and undaunted.*
That's the one I wanted to quote.
Sorry, I had to mix up.
So the line that caught my eye, yours too probably, is "does not produce a thought of fatigue."
The special emphasis of the Prajnaparamita teachings is our deeply ingrained faulty views.
That's what these teachings emphasize.
Actually, there is no such thing as fatigue.
And one of the things you notice in sesshin is you're feeling really, really tired and you say, oh my God, it's only the first day and I'm exhausted.
I'm going to be twice as tired tomorrow and three times as tired the next day.
How am I ever going to get through this?
I'm so tired.
And you're kind of dragging yourself along.
And then about an hour later, you're full of energy.
You feel great.
Nothing happened.
You didn't take any substances or change anything.
You didn't take a rest.
But the fatigue goes away.
So don't have any ideas of fatigue or any ideas about what your body can and cannot do.
Of course, sometimes the body cannot do something.
If you don't sleep for a really, really long time, your body is going to be tired.
If you don't eat, if you're pretty old, if you're ill or injured, if you exert yourself for long, long hours without taking a rest, the body will behave accordingly, naturally.
And this is the body's great pleasure.
This is the body's wisdom, to express itself according to conditions.
So of course we pay attention and we adjust the body.
We take a nap or we go to bed or we decide that it's time to give up mountain climbing and downhill skiing because we're 92.
But all these things are part of the practice of virya paramita.
Virya paramita doesn't just look like various people running up and down like a person, fully practicing with their body.
There's no fatigue.
There's no illness either.
There's just the body and its responses and our resolute practice with it.
That's what the sutra is trying to teach us.
And there's a big difference there.
Verse 29.
*Understanding that emotional reactions are dismantled by insight, supported by stillness, cultivate meditative stability that passes right by the four formless trances.
This is the practice.*
So this verse references the two classical aspects of meditation practice, insight or understanding, and stillness or concentration.
And zazen includes both.
Sometimes one, sometimes the other, sometimes both at the same time.
The four formless trances are deep meditation states we are conversant with, but we pass right by them.
We don't get excited about them or even particularly notice them.
But we know how important it is to still the mind, so that we can develop a depth of understanding.
And since this text is about bodhisattva practice, our emotional reactions that ruin our relationships with others are emphasized.
Meditation practice with its stillness brings us to understand these emotional reactions for what they are.
Like everything else that troubles us, they source in self-clinging.
And through our meditation practice we see that very, very clearly.
And seeing it, we're not so caught up anymore.
Working with such reactions carefully is the practice of ethical conduct.
Seeing through them and understanding them at their root is the fruit of meditation practice.
Paramita in 8,000 lines says,
*Those of great might who dwell in the four trances but do not make them into a place to settle down in, nor into a home.
But these four trances with their limbs will in their turn become the basis for the attainment of the supreme and unsurpassed enlightenment.*
So this verse affirms the importance of meditation for the bodhisattva path.
You would think, and some people think this way, that if our commitment as bodhisattvas is to benefit others, who has time for meditation?
It's like, why don't you spend every possible moment being of benefit?
Meditation, what could it have to do with benefiting others?
But bodhisattvas see the big picture here.

They can't help but notice that in the wealthiest nation the world has ever seen, where there is plenty of material support, political and social freedom, there is a lot of suffering and bitterness and confusion.
It's obvious to bodhisattvas that material and social support cannot be enough.
It's not enough.
In order to ultimately benefit beings, awakening is necessary.
Real wisdom and transformation and compassion is necessary.
Only supreme, unsurpassed awakening can save beings in the end.
So bodhisattvas practice meditation with the motivation of serving and helping.
They know that intense meditation practice is an essential ingredient in their path as bodhisattvas.
I'll read the verse on meditation from the Prajnaparamita.
I'm getting myself confused here.
I quite know what's going on.
The practice of concentration from 8,000 lines.
Yeah, I did.
I read that, didn't I?
Yeah, I did read it.
What's wrong with you people?
I thought I was confused.
Those are great minds who dwell in the four trances.
Yeah, I read that.
It's going on a long time here.
We've got to be in the last verse, right?
We are at the last one, right?
We did it, almost.
Yes.
All we have to do is sign here.
*Without wisdom, the five perfections are not enough to attain full awakening.
Cultivate wisdom and skill.
Free from the three domains, this is the practice of a bodhisattva.*
And this verse says nothing, actually, about Prajnaparamita at all.
I think that's because Tokme Zangpo figured out that of course his readers already know all this stuff.
They read all the Prajnaparamita sutras, so he doesn't have to say anything about it.
All he's saying is just notice that the five perfections already mentioned all come alive and serve as true bodhisattva practice only when they are perfumed by Prajnaparamita.
So, certainly it's a good idea to practice generosity, ethical conduct, patience, joyful effort, meditation, no matter what.
These are good things to do.
If we practice these things, we will definitely improve our lives and the lives of others around us.
But when we practice generosity and so on, pervaded by Prajnaparamita, we will bring light to the world.
We will be inspirations for our families and our communities.
And we can help to bring about a better world that we will know for sure is coming.
Here's what Ken, of course, puts a commentary to each of these verses himself.
In his commentary to this one, he says, how do you do this?
The same way that you get to Carnegie Hall.
How do you get to Carnegie Hall?
Is it over there?
Where is it?
I'll tell you the way.
Practice, practice, practice.
So, how do you do this?
The same way you get to Carnegie Hall.
Practice, practice, practice.
Learn the skills.
Then practice until they become second nature.

In that hymn, the perfection of wisdom is personified, is referred to here as the mother of all the Buddhas, the source, the matrix of all the Buddhas.

She is the source, and from everyone in the triple world she removes darkness. Most excellent are her words. The perfection of wisdom that cognizes the emptiness of all dharmas is not a cold and abstract, spiritual, intellectual achievement. It is warmth. It is love. It is healing.

It is protection. It is the salvation of the world for the one who practices it, as well as for everyone else. So, we have our marching orders. We know what we have to do when we leave Session. We know exactly what our practice is, what our commitment is. So, I wanted to just review it with you,

because you all know this, everything I said, everybody knows already. I want to just review it with all of you just on this seventh day of Session. So, thanks everyone very much for listening to me, drone on all week long with such generosity, such patience, and such energy. Hardly anyone fell asleep.

And I do appreciate, as you well know, I appreciate your practice very, very much. And I am so proud of what we have done together, not only these seven days, but over the years in our many sanghas. And I know that we will continue to practice on and on and on, until we straighten out this mess.

So, I will close with a few very short lines from the greatest religious poet, I believe the greatest religious poet of all time, Emily Dickinson. If I can stop one heart from breaking, I shall not live in vain. If I can ease one life, the aching, or cool one pain,
or help one fainting Robin, unto her nest again.
